speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am prepared to yield to the mover of Motion No. 2, but I also intend to take part in the debate on these amendments.
Perhaps we should consider the historical context, Madam Speaker, to have a better understanding of the scope of the amendments before the House.

On December 12, 1989, members of the House will remember that many of us were surprised, to use the term mildly, to hear from RCMP Commissioner Norman Inkster that 15 parliamentarians were currently being investigated by the RCMP: 11 were being investigated for alleged Criminal Code infractions and 4 others for
November 30, 1990

alleged election law violations. The revelation broke with traditional RCMP policy of not commenting on investigations while they were under process and before charges were laid. It many of us, to say the least.
The press coverage at the time reflected the reaction of many parliamentarians, including myself. It is no exaggeration to say that we were somewhat angered by the news, given that the conduct of police investigations, whether or not a conviction results, can hinder and, we can appreciate, can ruin a parliamentary career. Just the fact that one is under investigation by the police leaves a bad taste out there. We always believe that elected officials should be open to scrutiny and should be available to answer questions, but we never suspected that the police forces would reveal to the public of Canada that indeed they were investigating 15 Canadians. That kind of created a situation in this House that was requiring of some actions. The House felt it was in its good judgment to strike the committee. The committee looked at this whole situation and the possibility of reforming or amending the laws dealing with this House and the Senate in a way to make them more possibly adaptable to modem circumstances.
We also appreciate-and I am sure, Madam Speaker, you will understand-the changing times and the reform of the House following the McGrath commission report. The McGrath commission suggested in-depth reform of our procedures and our practices here. It gave the Board of Internal Economy, which is the administrative body of the House of Commons composed in the old days of strictly ministers of the Crown, an enlarged composition. It included members of the opposition on the new board, gave it new powers, and changed the whole way it operated.
Members of the House were surprised to hear all of a sudden that the rules of the game we had changed here were being interpreted by way of a manual of instructions as to what members interpreted in terms of the expenditures that they were allowed to administer their offices and render their services as elected representatives to the people of Canada. Therefore, the manual was becoming some kind of bible for the police, and the
Government Orders
interpretation of some of those sections was indeed difficult and possibly misleading to many people.
Therefore we took it upon ourselves that we should amend the Parliament of Canada Act. One of the important subjects that we had to deal with was the role of the board in determining what expenditures would be allowed under the budgetary expenditures of members of Parliament authority. Another important factor was how we could make sure that police forces and the justice system operate in an open, fair and just manner.
We recognize the duty of the police to investigate possible charges of misuse of public funds by MPs. Unfortunately some members of Parliament have abused the system. We recognize that this is far from being a perfect world and that the House of Commons is a reflection of Canada as a whole. The system is there, and sometimes people abuse it. We must have checks and balances. We did not want to impede in any way the justice system and how it operates.
We also had to balance the privileges we claim as members of Parliament to decide how to use the funds allocated to the members to represent their constituencies in an open and fair manner.
The committee looked at many things. We narrowed in on the authority of the board's rulings and opinions as to why or how the members should be expending public funds. We had to deal with a very difficult subject. I must admit that it took some time for many of us to make clear to our colleagues in the committee that we were not trying to impede police work but that we were trying to make it possible for members of the House of Commons and the Senate to obtain from the board clear and written opinions, directives that are easy to interpret, as to how we could expend the moneys in trust to us for administering our offices on the Hill and in the constituencies.
We dealt with a very contentious article at the time, which indeed many of us felt could be improved and was improved eventually. The motions and amendments before us today, as well as the bill as amended in committee, reflect an awful lot of understanding by all members in relation to the important matters as to how

November 30,1990
Government Orders
the funds will be expended, who has jurisdiction over the expenditures, how members of Parliament are to behave in terms of getting instructions from the board as to what is available, and how such things should be done.
Motion No. 2 indicates that members of the board who participate in the exercise and the powers of the board shall not be held personally liable for the actions of the board. The rest of the amendments all deal with the specific exclusive authority of the board to determine exactly how members of Parliament spend the funds made available to them.
We have reached a fair compromise. We have reached a good balance in terms of allowing police forces to ask the board-it is permissive, I admit; they do not have to, but if they want to have a good case I think they should-for an opinion if it is alleged that a member of Parliament has misused the funds that he or she has to administer his or her offices. In turn, if the police force gets an opinion from the board, that officer must make it available to the judge when in the process it has asked for either a warrant or the police force believes that it has reasons to require more information and wants a search warrant or something else. That opinion must be made available because it is essential to the process. We want it to be open. We want it to be as clear and limpid, if I may use that word, as possible. We also want to make sure that it is fair. To be fair, I think police forces now have the facility to ask the Board of Internal Economy for an opinion as to the expenditures of funds.
I hope all members of the House would take very seriously that members of Parliament who have doubt, who want a directive or need to be told more clearly how to interpret a certain rule or a certain disposition, should in turn ask the board for an opinion before they dispense public funds. Possibly we have allowed for a little more largess, if I may use that word. We have allowed for past expenditures to be included in that. Sometimes things change and sometimes there are oversights; members did not think about it or did not know about it. The amendments would allow that members to ask for an opinion from the board on past expenditures, on present expenditures, and on future expenditures.
If members ask the board for its advice, I am sure we will have little difficulty in keeping this place open and clearly in public view. I do not think that anything in these amendments could be seen or could be taken as an effort of the House of Commons and the Senate to put themselves above the law.
We are trying to maintain a system here of transparence.
[Translation\
We are not here to draft special legislation for members. We are here to try and clarify the situation, and the amendments we have before us do just that.

Madam Speaker, the Special Committee on the Parliament of Canada Act, which subsequently became the Legislative Committee on Bill C-79, met about fifty times, with some sittings lasting two or three days. During that time we saw committee members make a special point of being present themselves, despite changes in their duties. For instance, I went from being a Conservative Member to sitting as an independent member, and I am now with the Bloc quebecois, but I am still a member of the committee.
The Deputy Speaker of the House chaired the committee, and this was an honour for the committee. He was appointed minister, but continued to chair the committee nevertheless. The Government Chief Whip, the House Leader and the opposition's Chief Whip, people with extremely important duties here in the House, decided to spend an enormous amount of time-over 50 meetings-on this committee, to deal with an extremely difficult problem that arose last year. It does not make life easy for members when they are told by the Chief Commissioner of the RCMP that 15 members of Parliament are under investigation. Fifteen members means 5 per cent. If we apply this percentage to the population of Canada, it would mean that about one million people are under investigation. There is something disproportionate about all this.
We asked ourselves: Where is the problem? And throughout the proceedings of the committee, for one year, we enjoyed the extraordinary co-operation of the Clerk of the House and his staff-especially Mr. Kirby- and also the co-operation of the Chief Administrator of the House, Mr. Riedel and our Law Clerk and Parliamentary Counsel, Mr. Pelletier, with their respective teams. Without them it would have been impossible to finish the job.
Fifteen members of Parliament under investigation, and a year later, I don't think a single one has been convicted-maybe one. In most cases, investigations did not lead to charges being laid. In some case, charges were laid but were ultimately dismissed by the court. In some cases, there were searches, but the court subsequently decided that there had been no grounds for authorizing a search. In all cases, however, irreparable harm was done, not to the member personally, because
November 30, 1990

there is always the possibility that compensation might be discussed, but irreparable harm was done to the voters who gave this person a specific mandate, because his ability to represent his riding, his constituents, in the House of Commons has been diminished.
We must consider, Madam Speaker, that a member, who suddenly is the subject of a public inquiry or allegations by the RCMP, can hardly be expected to be able to perform his duties as well as any other member. Obviously, it hampers the member in his ability to act as a member here in the Parliament of Canada as well as in his own riding. Fifteen of our colleagues were in this kind of situation. For most of them, it was like being the subject of a public inquiry. Their names were all over the newspapers.
This means that hundreds of thousands of Canadians were represented by members whose powers had been diminished because a police officer happened to decide to conduct an investigation, often as a result of allegations by a political enemy or whoever. However in most cases, absolutely nothing was found. However, reputations had been sullied, constituents had not been well represented, or not as well as they would have wished, and we definitely had an abnormal situation.
Where is the problem? Madam Speaker, I think there are two sides to this question. Members of the House of Commons, as represented by the Board of Internal Economy, have not done a good job of being absolutely open about their activities. The Board of Internal Economy, which is supposed to represent them, has operated like a private, exclusive club that does not have to act with the openness that we tend to demand of this type of organization today.
The Board of Internal Economy revealed its decisions to no one. They did not become public until they were tabled in the first ten days of the following session, and in some cases this meant three years later. How could a member have personal knowledge of a decision of the Board of Internal Economy if it was not made public until three years later? And how was a Canadian citizen, an officer of the peace or an RCMP officer supposed to know about the decision? He did not, through no fault of the RCMP. It wasn't the fault of the average member of
Government Orders
this House but of the Board of Internal Economy which had not done its job. The bill will remedy this.
Perhaps some background information would be in order. Formerly, the Board of Internal Economy consisted only of members of the government in power. It consisted of the Speaker of the House and four government ministers. However, as part of the 1985 parliaments reform, it was decided to make the Board less partisan, and membership was changed to include two members of the Official Opposition and one member of the third party in the House of Commons, so that today, we can say that the Board fairly adequately represents the members of this House. There is good representation, Madam Speaker, but the Board neglected to change its rules of procedure and create a secretariat, for instance. It forgot to appoint someone to act on behalf of the Board. It did not have the power to adopt by-laws and it did not publish them.
We had police officers who argued, showning their complete ignorance of the role of a member of Parliament, that a member was like a public servant. That is false, Madam Speaker. A member is not a public servant. A public servant can ask permission from his superior. But as a member of Parliament, whom do I ask for permission? I have said repeatedly, and I still say, that I take orders from no one except from the people in my riding. I have no superior. There is not a single member in this House who can claim to be my boss, certainly not! I am here on behalf of the people of my riding, in a very special situation. No other Canadian citizen has those duties.
So we are not public servants, as RCMP officers and peace officers in general say we are. Madam Speaker, even the Chief Commissioner told the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General on December 12, 1989, that he did not know the Parliament of Canada Act.
He did not know what the Parliament of Canada Act was all about. On the other hand, he said that there were 15 members of Parliament being investigated because of expenses made under the Parliament of Canada Act. You can imagine that we ended up in a real mess: the Board of Internal Economy, which has rules which are not published; a RCMP officer who thinks that a member of the House is a civil servant; a RCMP officer who refers to the explanation manual, which is neither the Act nor the Regulations, and who decides to institute proceedings against 15 members of the House and the

November 30,1990
Government Orders
Senate. That was quite a mess. That is why we ended up with so many people. That is also the reason why I moved all these amendments which are not mine alone. I discussed these amendments with the other committee members and they were in agreement.
To summarize, if I may, the whole legislation that we wanted to introduce would try to solve the problem in two ways. On the one hand, in the future, the Board of Internal Economy would have a secretary under the Head Clerk of the House of Commons. It would get a sort of a head office. There would be a person there to whom people could address their complaints and where members could direct questions. There would be someone there. There would be an office.
Second, the Board of Internal Economy would have the power to draft its own administrative regulations. That was necessary.
Third, the Board of Internal Economy would have to publish its decisions within thirty days whether the House is sitting or not. People would no longer have to wait as long as three years. If its members agreed, the Board of Internal Economy would have the power to straighten out a situation which it should not have allowed to deteriorate that much.
On the other hand, the RCMP will of course continue its investigations of members of Parliament, except that, before starting one it should begin by looking into the Act, and I will make sure that it does by personally sending a copy of it to Mr. Inkster, for I should like him to read section 52.6 which reads as follows:
The Board -
-meaning, the Board of Internal Economy-
-has the exclusive authority to determine whether any previous, current or proposed use by a member of the House of Commons of any funds, goods, services or premises made available to that member for the carrying out of parliamentary functions is or was proper, given the discharge of the parliamentary functions of members of the House of Commons, including whether any such use
is or was proper having regard to the intent and purpose of the bylaws made under subsection 52.5(1).
(2) Any member of the House of Commons may apply to the Board for an opinion with respect to any use by that member of funds, goods, services or premises referred to in-
-a previous sub-section.
The Board of Internal Economy, therefore, has the power. Will it exercise it? As members of this House, we will deal with this issue later on. I hope so. It has to. It has the legal and moral obligation to do so, not only in the interest of the members of this House, but of all Canadians. So the police officer who is informed by a citizen-in bad faith in those cases, but often in good faith-that the member has committed an infraction concerning his budget will now be able to go the Board of Internal Economy and seek an opinion on the matter. If the officer is acting in bad faith and wants to act without going through the Board of Internal Economy, then the board will send him the opinion if he does not have the courage to seek it himself. But once the police officer has the opinion, served by whoever, he will be legally obliged to send it to the judge to whom he will submit any kind of legal request-search warrant, wiretapping, accusation, another warrant-and that is spelled out in the legislation. And not a justice of the peace but a judge so that members of Parliament will not be above the law. But members will be protected in the sense that the judge will have to take into account the opinion of the Board of Internal Economy which authorizes our expenses. If it authorizes our expenses, it will say whether the expense was correct or not.
Madam Speaker, that was the object of the amendments, most of them presented on behalf of the members of the committee, and I thank them all. In conclusion, I would say to my colleagues that what is being proposed today is probably the best piece of legislation we could have. It had been suggested to include something like "notwithstanding any section of the Criminal Code". That did not respect the principles which must guide us here in the House of Commons. But this bill provides enough guarantees for members, if the Board of Internal Economy does its job and if the RCMP act in good faith in their investigation by calling upon the Board of Internal Economy.
November 30,1990

Madam Speaker, I too wish to speak to the bill. At the end of June when this bill received second reading I, on behalf of the New Democratic Party caucus, rose to explain that we could not accept the bill as it was worded at that time.
The wording at second reading certainly gave a different situation from the bill than is before us in its amended form today. At that time the bill required an investigating officer to go before the Board of Internal Economy to get the opinion of the board before that officer received a search warrant or took any of the actions among those listed in the bill.
It did not stop an investigation, but if that officer did want a search warrant, did want a wiretap, or did want to take some other action, he or she was required to go before the Board of Internal Economy. The board then had 30 days in which to respond. That created, quite legitimately in my mind, a number of concerns. First, that we were being treated differently from other citizens in Canada and, second, that there was every opportunity, if an investigation was going on and an officer had to come to the Board of Internal Economy, there might be a leak and an investigation could be interfered with in that manner.
I do not think it was ever the intent of members of the House to tamper with a legitimate RCMP investigation. What we wanted was to cover some of the problems that had occurred as a result of the investigations which have gone on in the past and were referred to earlier.
Also, as a result of having the Commissioner of the RCMP appear before us a number of times, we heard that he and his officers had a number of problems when it came to dealing with members of Parliament. For example, if a complaint was made against a Canadian citizen with regard to a possible fraud or misuse of funds, then it would be normal for the investigating officer to go to the department concerned or the employer of that person. Through that means, the RCMP would probably receive the information it needed to determine whether an investigation should go forward.
The RCMP and the Commissioner appearing before our committee indicated that when it was a member of
Government Orders
Parliament, and with our perceived parliamentary immunity in a number of areas, the RCMP believed it was necessary to get a search warrant in order to get any information with regard to what was going on within the budgetary controls or in the offices of a member of Parliament.
They themselves suggested that we look for some other mechanism which would enable the RCMP to do its duties and at the same time respect the traditional rights of members of Parliament to do their work, not only as members of Parliament, but on behalf of their constituents. Often, we have very confidential information in the same way as a lawyer or a doctor would, because people have come to us expecting us to act on their behalf on issues which are very important and confidential to them. They are often in areas of complaints against the RCMP and certain government officials.
Often, as members of Parliament, we act as ombudsman for our constituents. If those files can be opened, without any protection, then it is not just members of Parliament who would feel threatened, but, obviously, any constituent or citizen of Canada who was working through a member of Parliament who could find that those files would be in the public domain.
There was a need to balance our rights on behalf of ourselves and on behalf of our constituents and other Canadians, and at the same time, to allow the RCMP and other investigating authorities the information they require in order to conduct an investigation or even to discover whether or not an investigation is required.
As a result of the very long and often repeated committee discussions and deliberations, the bill we have now balances those two concerns. Our constituents are protected, but at the same time the RCMP is able to go forward, just like any other law enforcement agency, and get the information it requires. There is no way, with the wording of the amendments that have come forward today as a result of the most recent committee deliberations, that we are inhibiting an investigation.
Now an RCMP officer or another investigator has the right, if he or she chooses, to go to the board and get information that they may require. That is their option. It is not a decision that is imposed upon them.

November 30, 1990
Government Orders
I know, Madam Speaker, that my time has lapsed for this particular part of the debate. I will explain later some of the other ramifications of the legislation at the appropriate time.

Madam Speaker, the House will be aware that in committee review of the legislation a new clause was added to the bill, which is an unusual procedure. Normally, it would not be allowed in this manner. However, as a result of events that have occurred over the last little while, there is a feeling that members of the board often dealt with matters that should remain in private.
There is, I think, in the case of any board of directors or any management group, a need to have some matters dealt with in private and in confidence. However, the wording that came down from committee was not acceptable to our caucus. I had indicated so during the meetings of the committee. Therefore, we have put forward this amendment, which I understand will be agreed to later on today, which helps to clarify and restrict those areas in which the Board of Internal Economy would have the right to expect its members to keep confidences.
To be more clear on that matter, I will refer to some of the areas. The amendment states:
-The oath or affirmation-relates to matters of security, employment and staff relations, tenders and investigations in relation to a member of the House of Commons and nothing in subsection (5) shall be construed as preventing the communication of any information relating to other matters to a party caucus."
The Board of Internal Economy has a right and obligation to make certain decisions behind closed doors. It cannot discuss the relations of an employee in public. That is not fair to the board, but more importantly, it is not fair to the employee. In terms of matters of security of the House of Commons and the people working in the House of Commons, again, it would not do much for security matters to have them discussed in public. However, I do remind people that it would have to be real security matters and not just perceived security matters or matters of inconveniences which often occur in the House of Commons or on the grounds of Parliament. They have to be matters of real security before the oath could bind members of the Board of Internal Economy.
November 30, 1990

For those areas, and for the purposes of collective bargaining, the board does need the right to expect that its members will not break confidences.
However, there are a number of other areas in which the board is the servant of the individual members of the House and the members of the various caucuses. We have to expect as members of Parliament that we have a right to go to our board members and ask what is happening on areas that we have raised with the Board of Internal Economy. As mangers of our own offices, we have been asking for computers and we have been asking for clarifications of travel rights and privileges within our own riding. We have the right to go to our board members and get that type of information.
We have, I think, through the amendment put forward, guaranteed the right of the board to deal with those matters that they must deal with behind closed doors. However, we have made sure that the oath is not so encompassing that it binds members of the Board of Internal Economy to perpetual silence on matters that should be in the public domain. In addition to that, it prevents the board members from becoming so isolated from the other members of the House of Commons that they no longer work on their behalf, serve them, and communicate with other members of the House of Commons.
I hope that the wording proposed here will resolve that problem. I hope it will receive the support of all members of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to move for third reading of a bill that has been discussed on more than 50 occasions by the Special Committee on the Review of the Parliament of Canada Act. At this time, I would like to thank committee members, especially the Whips of all three parties, the hon. member for Churchill who was whip at the time, the Official Opposition Whip who was subsequently promoted and is now Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, the
government's Chief Whip, and also another member who has done an extraordinary job since the committee started its proceedings, the hon. member for Megantic- Compton-Stanstead.
Madam Speaker, I also wish to thank the committee's research staff, especially Margaret Young and Jimmy Robertson, who did an excellent job for us for many months; the principal Clerk of the Committee, Mr. Kirby; and Mr. Sandy Birch, and also the many lawyers on Mr. Pelletier's team whom we consulted since we started our proceedings; Diane Davidson, and Gabriel Lapointe, who was hired by the committee.
As we all know, this bill represents a consensus formed by all members of this House and of the witnesses who appeared before the committee. I think we seldom have before us a bill as important as this one, and, as we saw in Hansard, a bill that was debated in this House with a complete absence of political partisanship.
I would like to thank all members who participated as well as the witnesses who appeared before the committee, and I would also like to say, Madam Speaker, that although today we are discussing Bill C-79, that does not mean the committee's work is finished. The committee still has a number of questions to consider, and we will continue to hold our meetings. In fact, the next item on the agenda is the matter of disclosure of funds made available to members.
We still have a lot of work to do, and I hope that my colleagues and I will be able to table many more reports and that these, like our first five reports, will receive the unanimous consent of this House.
I would also like to tell my honourable colleagues in this House that, when I say the bill was obtained by an exceptional consensus, I tell the truth. I would like especially to quote the words of the RCMP commissioner. We all know, as the member from Ottawa-Vanier said before, as well as the member from Megantic- Compton-Stanstead and the member from Churchill, that this committee was established after the RCMP commissioner said a number of members of Parliament were under investigation. After studying the bill, the commissioner appeared twice before our committee. I would like to quote the words he used during his testimony on September 25th:



November 30,1990



-where the commissioner says: "On a closing comment, Mr. Chairman, that, as the commissioner of the RCMP, I am absolutely delighted with all the work that has been done, with all of the attempts towards self-regulation, with all of the attempts to clarify the privileges and the disbursements to which members of Parliament have entitlement. I think all of that will go a long way to clarifying the issues of concern."

So, I would also like to thank the RCMP and its commissioner for their co-operation with the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to join the minister in thanking all of those who helped us and who worked hard to try to keep the committee productive. I think that, inadvertently, the minister may have forgotten to mention some members who worked with us for several months. I simply wanted to mention my good friend, and his good friend, Marcel Prud'homme, the member for Saint-Denis, Howard Crosby, the member for Halifax West, and Dorothy Dobbie, the member for Winnipeg South. There is also Mr. Iain Angus who, from time to time, was standing in for Mr. Murphy. To all these people, to all these colleagues of the House, I would like to extend my many thanks, because they helped me to perhaps understand a little better the solutions to the problems that seemed to be of concern to us all around this time last year.
Madam Speaker, I would have some comments to make. First of all, I want to make things clear. The situation is not the same anymore. Once the bill is passed, Madam Speaker, the Board of Internal Economy will have some work to do, some challenges to meet. And I want to put on the record right now in the House that, as a member of the Board of Internal Economy, I will take my responsabilities. We will do all we can to try to respond to the expectations in the bill and to give members the views that they will ask for. We will also give them the support that they need to make sure that, in all cases, we are straightforward and totally capable of meeting the challenge, that is, that the Canadian public must be satisfied that their representatives work openly and do not hide behind systems, laws or measures that could perhaps protect them.
Government Orders
Madam Speaker, nowadays people have a veiy cynical attitude towards politics, and that is unfortunate. But there is one thing I know for sure, we are going to work very hard in this House, on both sides of the House, to correct that, to restore confidence and to change the atmosphere, so that people will not see politics as something dirty. In politics, the citizens chose some people to represent them to the best of their ability. We are not perfect, but we do our best. As far as I am concerned, I want to say, on behalf of our caucus, that we will do our best to try and be as open as we can, Madam Speaker, so that Canadians know there is no partisanship on either side of the House, that we are open, that we can all say:
We are not here to get rich, or to abuse the system, we are here to serve the Canadian people and this is the way we want to be seen. We want to put an end to the cynicism so apparent in the media and in the public towards politics. That has to stop, Madam Speaker, and that is why this bill is so important. The bill will give hon. members a well-known, easy-to-manage system, as well as the transparency and responsibility all of us have been looking for.
Having said that, I am sorry I got carried away a little, but it is so veiy important that this bill be considered as a major piece of legislation, quite essential for the proper management of our country.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, throughout the entire exercise, I think this is the first time I have stood in the House relating to Bill C-79, but I spent many hours in committee. I am going to spend just a few minutes with my colleagues in the Chamber today.
In many ways in my eleven and a half years in the Parliament of Canada, this has been the most difficult assignment that I have accepted on behalf of the Chamber itself because you cannot move a word, comma or whatever in relationship to this bill without dealing with a conflict of interest. It is the bill which guides our lives as members of Parliament and members of the Senate.

November 30,1990
Government Orders
It is a statute that deals with the House of Commons and our responsibilities within it. In particular, the amendments that are proposed in Bill C-79 deal with our utilization of public funds on behalf of what we hope is a strengthening of the democratic process rather than a weakening.
It has been an exercise for me. There is a tendency to want to speak about the bill and all the marvellous things that it will do, including providing greater clarity to members and society, things that my colleague has mentioned. I am going to spend most of my time today talking about this experience in relation to the press and the role of journalists in our society related to an institution this important in our society.
I would like to say to journalists' schools around the country that this may be a case study. Material in the last 12 months related to this issue would constitute case material for a university class. I say that somewhat knowingly because my career prior to coming here was as a university teacher and a full professor.
Out of the real world, Madam Speaker, you sometimes get your best learning material. I would challenge every editorial writer in the country to review their own conscience. When they write an editorial and say that Parliament is trying to pass a law that will stop the RCMP from investigating members of Parliament, I simply say to them: "Find something in the law that we are passing today or in the previous versions or in the June report of the committee, that was designed to stop the RCMP from investigating members."
They will not find it, because it does not exist.
That does not stop senior editorial writers and editors of newspapers and journalists in broadcast from telling Canadian people that is what we are about.
It makes me angry, but it also makes me sad.
I arrived in this place in May 1979, like most Canadians a believer in democracy and with a feel for the importance of democracy. In 19841 went to the United Nations for three months during the fall sitting of the General Assembly. I discovered that I knew nothing about the importance of democracy when I arrived.
By the end of three months, looking at a world body where most are not democracies and really getting a feel for what it would be like to live in a place that is not democratically run, I came back to this country with a different and, I hope, a better appreciation of the importance of democracy.
When you look at the way journalists have treated this issue, you see they are eroding and destroying the confidence of Canadians in their democratic institution. This Chamber in which I speak today is more important than any one of us is or could ever be, because it represents the hopes and aspirations and the dreams of Canadians.
It is the place where we try to resolve the very serious problems of the nation to provide a better future for our children and their children. When our character is attacked collectively or individually by people who do not know what they are talking about but who have absolutely no difficulty in writing or reporting the most nefarious kinds of things about members of Parliament, my blood boils and my democracy is weakened.
I do not know what we are going to do about that over time, but my natural inclination as a Conservative is always self-regulation. The journalists of this country and the journalism schools had better get off the mark and do something about the accuracy of reporting and editorial writing in this country.
Just because we choose to put our names forward in our communities, with a willingness to sit in public office, does not mean that our characters can be assassinated at will by the public press in this country. Throughout this exercise, that was done. Some of us in this Chamber aid and abet that from time to time in the heat of the moment, and that is wrong too. That is simply wrong. Democracy and the institution are far too important for us collectively to tolerate this ad infinitum.
This bill deals with a problem and I will say it as clearly as I can. The RCMP, without the passage of this bill, has to go through a court process with a judge and everything else and put all kinds of allegations in writing to be able to get the simplest piece of information from this democratic institution. That is nothing that anybody in this Chamber decided on; it is required by 100, 200 and 300 years of history. The publication of those allegations that go about behind the scenes in a search warrant is
November 30, 1990

destroying people's lives: families, kids, children, MPs- all kinds of people. They make a laughing stock of the RCMP itself sometimes, with the absurdity of what is alleged.
This bill and the motivation of every single member of the committee from the start was to provide a simpler, cleaner way for an investigator in our society to get information about the people in this institution. That will save the RCMP embarrassment, that will save the members' embarrassment, that will save the members' families embarrassment, and that will save the institution embarrassment in the final analysis. That is what it has been about. Anybody who tells you anything different, Madam Speaker, simply does not understand or has some other goal or motivation in life such as to sell a newspaper.
Some people believe to sell a newspaper is the finest goal they can have in life. Well, it isn't. A newspaper should be accurate. The journalists have a responsibility to discipline themselves in the name of accuracy.
That is in another sense what the bill is about. There is no way that police forces in this country can ignore an allegation made against a member of Parliament. They have an obligation to investigate. What this bill is about is giving them accurate information so that there is no misunderstanding that can arise and no damage that can be done.
I will end in just a few moments so that my colleagues can have their chance to say something, but I stand here with pride because I know how hard the members of the committee worked and under what difficult circumstances. The biggest sense of pride is the sense that we have almost unanimous approval of 293 very special people: leaders in their home communities who were selected by the voters of this country and sent here. To say that members of Parliament are like everybody else is nonsense. They are special. They were elected to be special. They are handed special responsibilities, and there is no greater responsibility than the protection of the democratic institution itself so that it can function and it can be self-correcting.
The bill we pass today is a contribution to that activity, to that goal and that end. I am pleased to have been able to be part of that process.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I was almost ready to get up and accuse the chief government Whip of filibustering the legislation.
I also wish to rise, at this time, to speak about the proposed legislation. I decided, more than a year and a half ago, that I was no longer going to serve as Whip of this caucus. Last December, a month before my term of office ended, I agreed to be on this committee for a few short weeks to clean up some problems that existed with the present legislation.
Here we are, one year later, and we are finally having the proposed legislation put through the House of Commons. I am glad to see that it has happened. I think it helps to clarify the role of the Board of Internal Economy and, more important, it helps to make sure that there are open investigations of members of Parliament that we as a House can provide information where it is required and we are not perceived to be impeding any investigation. I think that is very important.
I also think it is important that other parts of this legislation, which have received a lot less public scrutiny, have been put into place. It is important that the role of the board is clarified. It is important that the by-laws that the board enacts be tabled in the House of Commons, so that not only members of Parliament are aware of what the rules are but, in addition, the public is aware of them.
This committee was established with the intention of doing a few short weeks of work, but it has taken a long time. I would also like to point out, in the very few minutes I have left, that other things have to be done as well. The committee, in its deliberations, has dealt with some of the problems that we face. It has helped to ensure that the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services is revising the manual, which more or less sets the ground rules for how we spend money and what are legitimate usages of the public purse by members of parliament, and that is important.
That is very important ongoing work by members of that committee, because our bible, if one wants to call it that, had become archaic and had a number of clauses which were not only unenforceable but which denied the reality all of us faced. I always cringed when I saw lines in it which said that we should not use our printing privileges for partisan purposes, that we should not be using any of our privileges for partisan purposes. When I rise in the House, I quite often have some partisan purpose for doing so. I was elected as a member of one political party. I expect to get up and speak, on behalf of that particular, partisan viewpoint. If I do so, I also

Government Orders
expect that I will perhaps mail out literature stating that I am a New Democrat, that this is what I stand for, that this is what I believe, and that this is what I have said in the House of Commons on those very issues. We have helped to clarify some of the silly rules that we had in place. We have recognized that within limitations we are here as partisans and that we use our resources for legitimate communication of those partisan opinions to the public.
We also have other things which have to be done. The committee has recognized that it is important that we have disclosure of what we spend from the public purse and how that money has been spent. A lot of the problems we have faced result from the fact that the public does not have access to our information. Other legislatures around the world have a form of disclosure which enables the public to know what has been spent from public funds. It is only reasonable that happened for this House of Commons as well. I hope that the committee has the opportunity to finish its work in that area.
In addition, it is time that the government forced through tough, enforceable conflict of interest legislation. That should be in place. It is one of the things that will help to make sure the public understands that what we do is on behalf of the public, not for any personal benefit or gain.
There are things yet to be done, but I am proud of the work of the committee in the end. I also would like, in the very few seconds I have left, to thank the people who have worked on behalf of the committee, the researchers and others. I hope we will take a look at this legislation in a year's time. I hope we will not say that was the end of the process but that it was only the beginning of the process of helping to make sure that what we do in Parliament, how we spend money and we do on behalf of the public, is open to real and complete public scrutiny.

Madam Speaker, as we are coming to the end of
this debate, I will make a wish, a very important wish for democracy. I wish that policemen thoughout this country do their duty so that we never have to intervene into their role which is extremely important for democracy. But I also wish that members of Parliament, the House of Commons and the Senate, and the Parliament of Canada as a whole could do their duty without the improper interventions of the police or of a policeman in particular. However, the House of Commons as much as its members or the policemen will have to understand that this bill must take a little while to get over its teething troubles. I wish that policemen co-operate very closely with the Board of Internal Economy. I also want members to realize that self-discipline in any constituted body, including the House of Commons, is absolutely necessary and often convinces people who are watching us and all Canadians that it is as such the best guarantee.
I also ask that the Board of Internal Economy not seek unanimity all the time, but rather consensus. With the self-discipline we will all exercise together, I am convinced we will never again experience the problems we have been through lately.
I wish the Special Committee on the Parliament of Canada Act will immediately consider the whole question of total and complete disclosure of members of Parliament budget expenditures.

that Bill C-315, an Act to change the designations of the buildings known as Place du Portage, Phase I, II, in and IV, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I have the pleasure today to present this legislation to give a new designation to the buildings known as Place du Portage, Phase I, II, III and IV, located in the City of Hull.
I have accepted to present this private bill at the request of the City of Hull. This is an initiative led by city councillor Pierre Chenier and you are seeing today the outcome of a long process to change the present designation of Place du Portage because it does not reflect the specific nature of the buildings, but merely the construction stages of the complex. I must point out that, contrary to what some might be tempted to think, the names chosen by the City have nothing to do with political partisanship.
Representatives from the city of Hull wish that these buildings be now named after famous persons of national significance. So, it is with this in mind that they directed their research in order to submit the names of two famous persons who were involved in national politics and whose names would be consistent with the francophone reality of that city's territory. That is why they decided to choose Mr. Jean Marchand and Mrs. Therese Casgrain. The city council referred the matter to the Hull Identity Committee, a committee made up of elected representatives and citizens, which unanimously recommended the names of Jean Marchand and Therese Casgrain. The City of Hull received a lot of support for its choices, notably from the children of Mr. Marchand and Mrs. Casgrain.
Why Jean Marchand? People will remember that Jean Marchand, when he was the first Minister of Regional Economic Development, worked relentlessly to make
Private Members' Business
sure that the Quebec side of the National Capital would get some federal buildings. Jean Marchand was, indeed, the key architect of the decision of the Ottawa government to move to Hull one fourth of the federal Civil Service in spite of the indignation that you remember. It is even more important now to give this tribute to him because close to 21 000 federal civil servants work today on the Quebec side of the Ottawa valley. And, soon, when Quebec takes a decision concerning its political future, those jobs in the Outaouais will still be an important factor.
Why Therese Casgrain? Because she played an important role in our country by spending her life fighting in favor of women's right to vote and because she is considered a leader among 20th century Canadian women who advanced the cause of reform. Wouldn't it be a good occasion to pay homage to her also, particularly since we are celebrating this year the 50th anniversary of women's right to vote.
We must also take into account the fact that federal buildings in the National Capital Region are all identified with different names such as l'Esplanade Laurier, Louis Saint-Laurent, Jules Leger, Jean Thlon, Vanier, etc. To keep up with that spirit the city of Hull has made that request and also to avoid any confusion, as is the case with Place du Portage Phase I, n, III and IV. The Information Services sometimes receive many calls from people wanting to know the location of one of them.
Phases I and II of Place du Portage will now be known as Jean Marchand Building, South Tower, and Jean Marchand Buiding, North Tower. As for Phases III and IV, they will be known as Therese Casgrain Building, West Tower, and Therese Casgrain Building, East Tower. For all these reasons, I dare wish that my colleagues in the House of Commons will agree to refer this bill to a legislative committee, so that, before long, we can name these buildings on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River after these two great Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the federal level, the designation of public buildings is the responsibility of Public Works. There is nothing wrong with that, since it owns most government buildings.
As a matter of fact, Public Works is not only responsible for a hundred or so federal office buildings, but also for cultural centres, employment centres, research laboratories, harbours, farms and others facilities. Public

November 30, 1990
Private Members' Business
Works is also responsible for the accomodations used by 135 departments and agencies. In fact, some 150,000 civil servants go to work everyday in buildings Public Works is responsible for. Finding an appropriate name for the buildings is an important task it carries out with great care.
The policy on the designation of federal facilities is the following: Choose a prestigious name that will be readily recognized and respected; give recognition to one person or a group of persons who contributed to the well-being of Canada, the community or the customer department; finally, remind a historical event to the community or the client department.
This policy includes a number of criteria Public Works used to determine the merit of the proposals. For instance, it goes without saying that the person it is suggested to name a building after must be deceased, but it can also be named after a place or an event of historical importance, if there is a connexion between the name and the building. The names proposed must also have some prominence in the region.
It seems clear to me that the name Place du Portage is quite appropriate. It reminds us of the days when explorers travelled our rivers in canoes discovering Canada. It reminds us not only of those courageous explorers but also of traders and missionaries who travelled those rivers during decades. Place du Portage brings back to mind not only certain events but also a historic site and a lot of people instead of only two.
According to our policy on the names of federal buildings, any individual or group can make suggestions. Department officials can recommend a name themselves or ask for suggestions. These consulted persons could be the public in general, historical societies, historians, universities, municipal councils or people who have lived in the community for a long time and know the subject well. In the case of property acquired through a lease-option agreement, the promoter also has his say concerning the proposed name.
It is then up to the region's chief manager, an official of Public Works Canada, to check the proposition. To that end, he can consult with the Secretary of State, the Privy Council or any other ressource group he sees fit. The regional chief manager then presents a report on
the results of the study to the deputy minister, who in turn presents it to the minister.
Finally, it is the minister who decides if the name can be given to the facilities or building. At first sight, this system seems complicated or overly prudent. But the government believes that it is worth it, that it ensures that these assets are properly named. Once the name is chosen, it is extremeley difficult to backtrack. Also, a building's name should mean something and be appreciated not only by its tenants, but the community at large and all interested parties.
For years, Mr. Speaker, buildings have been named after distinguished Canadians. As mentioned by my colleague we have, in the National Capital Region, the Jules Leger Building and the Lester B. Pearson Building. I could mention the Champlain Maritime Terminal in Quebec City or the Guy Favreau Complex in Montreal, both named after famous Canadians. That does not mean that buildings are necessarily named after politicians. Many commemorate people who distinguished themselves in other fields of activity.
I suggest to my colleague who made some proposals here, today, Mr. Speaker, that he tells the group he represents-the City of Hull, that he mentioned a few times if I am not mistaken-that we could forget politicians and look for other names.
I am proposing that, Mr. Speaker, because as Mao said, women support half of the sky, but I noticed that in the political arena they are denied access to some fame which is justly theirs.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is high time that we recognize famous women and pay tribute to those who, in the end, contributed to the history of Canada and were part of it. It is clear that if we limit ourselves to politicians we would restrict the pool of names dramatically, since it is a well known fact that women gained access to this venerable institution only recently, when in reality women had a major role in the settlement and development of Canada.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I would like for my honorable colleague that he goes back to his constituents and suggests to them that they think about the role of women in our society, without restricting themselves to political roles, which would limit too much the pool of available names. And if he needs help finding names of
November 30, 1990

very important and distinguished women, I will personally assist him if his group can't. We have exceptional women in Canada as well as in Quebec.
In conclusion- I hear chauvinist comments, Mr. Speaker. I hope you did not hear them, because it is horrible to hear such things in 1990! I repeat, I find the name Place du Portage fully satisfactory. It is a very important historic site and, I repeat, I don't believe it is a good thing to change something just for the sake of it, especially according to the recommandations that have been made. I see no improvement whatsoever in it.
I would like to say finally that if the department wishes once more to change the building's name, I would hope it would choose something other than the name of a political figure. If my colleague would listen, I would suggest further that consultations be held not only in Hull, but elsewhere. Consultations should be held as well as studies made before a decision is taken on the matter.
I believe we should follow the process used previously, and succesfully, Mr. Speaker, under the supervision of different departments and several Public Works ministers.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, not only will I not support the motion, I say that the bill should be withdrawn.

Madam Speaker, the suggestion made today by the hon. member for Hull-Aylmer is very interesting. I think the Conservative member, who recommended that we should turn down this suggestion, call it a bill or a motion, based her remarks on a very simple argument. As far as I am concerned, I think it best to provide a building with a specific designation, in order to show the respect we have for people who have served this country. For all these reasons, this suggestion seems to me like a good idea.
And there is another reason for that as well, Madam Speaker. The Hull residents have themselves expressed the wish to change the designations of the Place du Portage buildings to honour the memory of Jean Mar-chand and Therese Casgrain. I do think personally that it is very fitting to honour these two key figures in this way.

For all of us, Madam Speaker, there is a concern to serve our community's needs and expressed concerns. In the case of this particular Private Members' Bill before us, if I understand the argument correctly, that is precisely what the member for Hull-Aylmer is attempting to do.
He is attempting to bring before the House something that will reflect the wishes of his community to see the two individuals of whom he has spoken, Jean Marchand and Therese Casgrain, showing the honour of which I think they are quite deserving for many reasons. They are reasons that have to do with the risks which they took in the fight for social justice in the Province of Quebec and with the contribution which both have made in the Parliament of Canada.
From my personal point of view, I am particularly pleased to see the suggestion that Therese Casgrain be given a sign of honour and respect here in the National Capital Region. Her work as a leader in the fight for women's rights in Quebec was, of course, extremely important. But her work as leader of the party which was the predecessor to our party, the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation, is also something which certainly I respect considerably, and which I think should be respected by people across the country. She was one of the very first women leaders of a political party anywhere
in the country and that was not a very easy task. It was not an easy task to be a path breaker.
The names that have been suggested by the community of Hull are appropriate names and names that deserve to be honoured. As a House of Commons, we should respect the expressed wishes of the community of Hull and accept the motion which has been put forward by the member for Hull-Aylmer, to have it pass to a legislative committee, and have representatives from the community of Hull come to speak to us about their reasons for this particular choice of names. I want to say to the hon. member for Hull-Aylmer, who is a reasoned and rational person, that he will know that is not automatically my position.
We look at the edifice that is across the river, a large structure of buildings, with that beautiful name. I am not sure what particular nuances it has for French-speaking Canadians, but I know that for English-speaking Canadians, names such as Portage la Prairie and Place du Portage have a very special ring for which we have a deep sense of our national history.
We know that the country was discovered from east to west along the highways of the rivers, the portages, and all that infers. It beckons back to the earliest days of the foundation of the country.
I would agree with the hon. member who spoke earlier, a member of the Liberal Party, who said that that whole complex should retain and contain that name, Place du Portage. But then we have these towers that I submit could only have been named after a national committee of accountants put together a thorough analysis and study and came up with the picturesque,
November 30, 1990

descriptive, and accurate titles of Tower I, II, III, and IV. I commend that presumed committee of accountants, wherever it might be, for its accuracy.
I submit that if there is anything that is in need in our country today, it is the need for national symbols that will make us hearken to and recognize the heritage and the great people who built the country. Names should be honoured and recognized.
I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that having looked at the names that have been put forward, I would want to make two comments. First, I would want the hon. member for Hull-Aylmer to know that in no way for either of those two names could I find any justifiable reason to say that those names ought not to be utilized. Second, if I could, it probably would be inappropriate for me to say no to those names to the hon. member who is the representative of that city, after his city council has said that these are the names that it wants. That would very much impinge on the local community from which he comes and which he represents.
I will, however, put forward this thought, because I think there is in the country a need to advance more symbols. There is a need to advance more recognition to our history. Instead of naming two towers for one person, here is a possibility to name all four towers after Canadians and for Canadians who have demonstrated purpose.
>
I am an advantaged member of this House because I sit right down at this end. I do not know which camera is on me at the moment, but if it is the far one, the pages will be seen right beside me.
In preparing to speak today, I turned to the pages and asked them to name for me a famous Canadian. They did. They said Rick Hansen. I asked them to name another one and they said Terry Fox. I asked them to name another, and they said Lester Pearson, then Billy Bishop, Karen Kain, Brian Orser, and Margaret Atwood. The civil service is going to go plum nuts when it hears this one. The hon. member for Prescott-Glengarry- Russell might even put the motion forward. They said Wayne and Shuster. How do you like that, Madam
Private Members' Business
Speaker? 'Where do you work?" "I am over at the Wayne and Shuster Building".
What I found intriguing about the list given to me by the pages is that of the nine names, one is a politician. It is important that politicians be recognized, but that it is also important that we recognize this country was built to a very large and significant extent, not by what took place in this building, but what took place as a result of men and women from all parts of Canada who helped to make the country great.
I know everyone in this House is sensitive to the fact that we have come through a tumultuous summer in terms of native affairs in this country. When I look at the situation with native persons in Canada and when I put in balance the fact that I know so many native leaders of extraordinary quality, of extraordinary skill, with far above average capacity for articulation, I am perplexed at why North America, both Canada and the United States, has so few native heroes.
We have Buffy Sainte-Marie, a folk singer who is nationally and internationally known. I put that in the context of the black movement in the United States. I was a student at the University of Montana. One of the most moving days of my life was to be in San Francisco among a group of 22,000 blacks to listen to a speech by Martin Luther King. It will, as long as I live, be a highlight of my life.
The blacks advanced to a significant extent because of national heroes in their country. The first such person was probably Jackie Robinson, the first black to play professional baseball. Today television broadcasts of Bill Cosby warms the hearts of virtually every person around the world. With national heroes, we soon do what we ought to do in race relations. We fail to see that the person's skin is a different colour. That is important.
Across the river in the city of Hull is probably one of Canada's proudest buildings, the Museum of Civilization. It will probably live with that name forever. It may be all too soon forgotten that that building was designed by an Albertan from my home province, a full blood native Canadian and one of Canada's most exceptional architects.

November 30,1990

It might well be in the community of Hull since we have four towers to name that there would be some appropriateness, especially in these times, to reach out and say to the native community: "We will place the name of one of your people on one of our national buildings". I submit that that consideration might be undertaken. I think of the name of the person who my constituency was named after, Crowfoot.
Chief Crowfoot was bom a Blood. He migrated north with his grandfather at the age of five, walking from what is now Montana into what is now southern Alberta. He became chief of the Black Foot and he adopted a Cree son, the first test of multiculturalism. That person, who spoke only his native tongue, at the time of the signing of treaty seven, spoke in English. He said this as an elderly chief: "In a little while I will be gone from among you. Wither I come and wither I go, I do not know. What is life? It is like the flash of the firefly in the night. It is like the breath of the buffalo in the wintertime. It is like the little shadow that races across the grass and loses itself in the sunset." That, by a nomad, who travelled with the buffalo, who learned the language late in mid life, to give that kind of poetic expression, written by the Northwest Mounted Police, needs somewhere in this country his name on an edifice, a building, to signal his importance.
I commend the hon. member for Aylmer-Hull. I simply ask that we only take that time to do the job fully and completely so that all towers can be appropriately named and that we enhance in the process the naming of more places after good Canadians, wherever they may come from.

Madam Speaker, I want to talk about Hon. Jean Marchand. The Hon. Member opposite said that she was against designating a building in honour of Hon. Jean Marchand. I am not imputing motives; the reason she is against it does not matter. What matters is that she is against it and for that, she should be ashamed of herself!
I have the rigth to say so in this House. I suggest she should be ashamed of herself for being against the designation of a building in honour of Therese Casgrain and Jean Marchand and I suggest that Hull-Aylmer constituents and all the other Canadians share my views, Madam Speaker. I am prepared to say so in front of anyone. The City of Hull has submitted an application through its elected representatives, and they are not just nobodies! They were people chosen by the Hull electorate both at the federal and municipal levels.
Here is part of the record of proceedings of a Hull Municipal Council meeting dealing deals with this issue. I should like to quote from a resolution adopted on March 20, 1990: "It is resolved that the council is asking the Government of Canada to designate Place du Portage, Phase I, as Jean Marchand Building, North Tbwer, Phase II as Jean Marchand Building, South Tower, Phase
III,	as Therese Casgrain Building, East Tower, and Phase
IV,	as the Therese Casgrain Building, West Tower".
The councillors of the city of Hull are the ones who asked for this, Madam Speaker. The federal representatives, more particularly the member for that riding, asked for this in the House and I had the privilege of seconding the motion in the House today.
If members opposite are against such a designation, let them say so. But in fifteen minutes, Madam Speaker, we will know for sure. If Conservative members decide not to allow us our right to vote on this motion today, that is
Private Members' Business
their privilege. They can kill the bill, talk it out. They might do it; that is their privilege.
And I would dare say that they do, it will only be for political partisanship. It is not mere coincidence that Mrs. Casgrain was a New Democrat, and Mr. Marchand a Liberal. A few years ago, when the time came to erect a statue in honour of Mr. Diefenbaker, I gladly supported the motion here in Parliament, and it was done. Two years later, we tried to do the same for Mr. Pearson, and what took just a few months for Mr. Diefenbaker took two years for Mr. Pearson. But we got our wish although it took much more time. I did not blame the government then because we finally got what we were asking for.
But today, Madam Speaker, what the Conservatives are displaying is partisanship of the worse kind. When I see the hon. member for Bourassa act as she did today, Madam Speaker, I am outraged. I hope the constituents from Hull and all Canadians, but especially women, will remember what the hon. member for Bourassa said today and the decision this House is about to make.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   PLACE DU PORTAGE BUILDINGS DESIGNATIONS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the name Place du Portage goes deep into the heart of the city of Hull as I understand, and for many people it invokes memories of the voyageurs who passed this way in quest of their furs and other riches as they moved westward and opened up this country.
The portage was, of course, the overland route taken to avoid the Chaudiere Rapids as the tradesmen moved up and down the Ottawa River.
Writing of the trail which the Indians used to cut off the long way around the bend in the river, the hon. F. R. Latchman said: "In order to get ahead of the voyageurs as they came up the river in their canoes, the Indian runners took a trail across the country, leaving the river at a point where the city of Hull now stands".
They bore northwesterly until they reached the mountain this side of the Eardley Line and then followed by foot across Eardley and thence to the river again.
By this means they could let their tribe know of the approach of the voyageurs as they came up and down the river. At first it was to prepare their tribe for a hostile reception of the voyageurs and later to meet them for

November 30, 1990
Private Members' Business
barter and trade in furs and do commerce with the voyageurs.
The traditional portage paths that skirted the Chau-diere Rapids were on the north shore. They first crossed the present day Eddy Company yards and at Little Chaudiere Rapids, a short distance upstream, another carry was necessary.
Today in the Hull suburb of Val-Tetreau, beside the Ottawa River and a short walk downstream from the statue of the martyred priest, Saint Jean de Brebeuf, there is a monument showing the old path over which the missionaries, explorers and traders trod.
Before the great days of the timber industry, many fortunes in furs were floated up and down the River.
As the traders went, settlers appeared, things changed.
In 1800 the arrival of Philemon Wright marked the beginning of the lumber trade which was to bring growth, prosperity and many fortunes to the area in the century that followed.
I mention these historical events because this history is very important in our country, important to this area, and important to all of Canada. Certainly the name Place du Portage sticks out.
The name was selected with care when the buildings were built. It preserves the memory of a stretch of ground that was important in the building of this country. It is a reminder to citizens of Hull and all of us in the national capital region of our beginnings and our heritage.
It is important that we do not in any way dilute or obscure the name Place du Portage as it relates to the complex of buildings which have transformed the city of Hull over the past several years to be a thriving, growing and important part of the national capital region.
The proposal put forward by the hon. member for Aylmer in Bill C-315 merits consideration. It is the practice of the federal government to name some government buildings after distinguished Canadians when such action is deemed suitable and doable.
As other speakers have pointed out, M. Marchand and Mme Casgrain both served with some major distinction in Canadian public life.
But in the case of Place du Portage I think it is important that no precipitous action be taken that might detract from the eminently suitable and well-established name that the complex now bears.
The name is well established and well known. Maybe it has some simplicity to it, as the member for Crowfoot mentioned, that they just went "one, two, three, and four", but it does sit well over-all with the citizens of the national capital region.
It is also a rather simple nomenclature. Place du Portage' is a very large complex and houses a myriad of federal government departments and agencies.
Its tenants include Supply and Services Canada, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Employment and Immigration Canada. It houses all or parts of the National Capital Commission-

Maybe it is kind of important and interesting that they do. You do, we do, because we are all here. It is amazing what other people do not know, so maybe it will not hurt to tell them what departments are there. Canada Post Corporation is there and so is Labour Canada, Public Works Canada and other departments and agencies, including Health and Welfare Canada, Agriculture Canada, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, and some of the offices of National Defence. In short, it is a microcosm of the federal government itself.
Over the past decade and a half, it has become a familiar address to thousands of Canadians who do business with the government and who receive services from the complex. Members of the public have a difficult enough time working out how and under what name they can reach a certain department or agency. All of us have problems now and again, and we work here every day.
We should be very careful to avoid making things even more complicated. I am not saying that changing the name is going to do that but I think we should think about all of this. The present nomenclature is quite clear, the complex is named Place du Portage and its main buildings are designated in a very simplistic way, I, II, III and IV. So I will expect, on this Friday afternoon, that he gives me the same respect.
The proposal put forward in Bill C-315, would add another layer to the designations already in place. It would call one building the Jean Marchand building, north tower and another the Jean Marchand building, south tower and the same in connection with Therese Casgrain. Then we get into east towers, west towers and that sort of thing.
It has been a consistent policy of the government that when buildings are named after specific persons, it gives the name only to one physical structure. That is the way it has been done. No one is saying that these particular names should not be used. It was suggested by the city of Hull and by the member of Parliament for Hull-Aylmer. I do not think anyone is indicating that these people are not great Canadians. But I think that giving two separate and distinct edifices the name of the same person might invite confusion so maybe we should think about this. For this reason alone, it could be that we should reflect upon it.
However, it does not mean that the government rejects out of hand, as maybe it was indicated by some people across the way, the idea of giving names of the prominent Canadians to these buildings. I do not think there would be any disagreement from members opposite that there are other important Canadians, other than politicians, some names were mentioned, for instance, by the Pages to the member for Crowfoot. I am sure if we gave the question to the young people of Quebec, they would come up with another long list that would have a lot of other names on it and they would not all be politicians.
In fact, the Prime Minister received a similar proposal from Le Cornell de la municipalite de la ville de Hull
Private Members' Business
earlier this year, as the hon. member probably knows, and he has referred it to the Minister of Public Works for his study and consideration. The minister, as members hopefully know, has the responsibility for the naming of federal buildings and structures and he will certainly do so.
This is not an undertaking that is entered into lightly by the government. I hope that we would all take that into consideration here today. It is normal for the matter to be thoroughly researched and that there be extensive consultation for the naming of buildings. Certainly the minister and the government will do that, taking into account the submission made by the city of Hull and the member of Parliament for that constituency and the discussions that were held here today.
A building is a thing of some permanence and it is important that all those directly affected have ample opportunity to express their views. For these reasons, and without precluding the possibility of assigning names to the structure at this point, the position of the government will be that we should take under advisement the names that have been put forward and look at naming all four buildings in the future.
Madam Speaker, I thank you veiy much for the opportunity to speak on this important bill put forward by the member from Hull.

Madam Speaker, I will be brief, because my colleague also wants to speak to this matter. I would like to make just one point. One of my first experiences in this field, when I was elected mayor of Beauhamois, was that people wanted to change the name of the Beauhamois Municipal Hall, which had been known as such since time immemorial, and it so happened that they wanted to name it after my political opponent who was the outgoing mayor of Beauhamois at the time. However, I had a good excuse which was that he wasn't dead yet and so they did not have the right to do that. However, I still felt somewhat guilty about possible political overtones, and that is what I have been feeling during the last fifteen or twenty minutes, and that is the point I wanted to make. Clearly, if someone had suggested that the four towers be named after four Indian chiefs and if we had opposed it, we would have been accused of being anti-Indians.

We have the names of two prominent Canadians, a man and a woman. I suppose that one can be accused of being "blue" and not "red", or of not willing to recognize the achievements of women. That is not true because I believe they both had a political career that I admire, and I would love, at some point, to have the political career they enjoyed.
Personally, I believe that we cannot make things simpler than they are now. Place du Portage, Phase I, II, III or IV, the name this complex has been carrying for 15 years now, might not be very poetic, but it seems easier to me than Jean Marchand North Tower, Jean Marchand South Tower, Therese Casgrain East Tower, Therese Casgrain West Tower. I used to be the Paliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and each year we received thousands of letters. There is also Employment and Immigration and Consumer and Corporate Affairs. All addresses would have to be changed. I was impressed by my colleague's speech earlier. I also think we should keep things simple and maintain some continuity. It has been there for 15 years and it should be kept for future generations. I am not saying that the proposed names do not mean anything, but I still think that what is being suggested lacks in simplicity.
I would have had more to say, Madam Speaker, but I will yield to my colleague who has a few words to say about this bill.
